chunks: A number of our companions, from Sahl ibn Ziyad, from Bakr ibn Salih, from Muhammad ibn Abi Hamza, from Uthman al-Asbahani, who said:

Ismail ibn Abi Abdillah (peace be upon him) gifted (something) to me, so I gifted to him a Ra'ibi bird (pigeon). So Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) entered and said: 'Place this Ra'ibi bird with me in the house, for it comforts me.'
He (the narrator) said, 'And Uthman said, I went to Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) and in front of him was a pigeon, and he was breaking bread for it.'

key_terms.طَيْراً رَاعِبِيّاً: A specific type of pigeon or dove, noted for its beauty or song
key_terms.يُؤْنِسُنِي: It comforts me / keeps me company

ai.seo_question: What does the hadith reveal about the Imams' relationship with animals and their daily life?
ai.summary: This hadith from *Al-Kafi* highlights the domestic intimacy of the Imams, specifically Imam Ismail ibn al-Imam (peace be upon him) and Imam Ja'far al-Sadiq (Abu Abdillah), who kept pigeons as pets for companionship and leisure. The detail of the Imam breaking bread for the birds underscores the concept of *mu'amalat* (social interaction) extending to animals, reflecting a gentle, approachable nature rather than mere utility. In Shia tradition, this serves as a model for kindness to creatures and the permissibility of keeping pets for enjoyment within the household.
